bellamy-looking-backward-1888.summary: In 1888 Bellamy's Looking Backward imagined the year 2000 with credit cards and no poverty; it sold a million copies and spawned clubs. Journalist Bellamy tells of Julian West, a young Bostonian who falls into hypnosis-induced sleep in 1887 and wakes 113 years later in a United States transformed into a socialist utopia; much of it is dialogue in which Dr. Leete explains that society to West by comparison with West's era. Over 162 Bellamy Clubs formed in the United States to spread its ideas.

bellamy-looking-backward-1888.detail: Its themes are problems of capitalism, nationalisation of all industry, and an "industrial army" to organise production and distribution. Everyone retires at 45 with full benefits, goods are bought with credit cards drawing on equal shares of national product, and sermons and music reach homes by cable "telephone". Initial sales were modest, but reviews in Boston papers helped it sell a million copies within a few years; historian Daniel Immerwahr says only Uncle Tom's Cabin sold more in its first years in nineteenth-century America. It inspired several utopian communities and influenced intellectuals and socialist writing of the day.

bertha-benz-drive-1888.summary: In August 1888 Bertha Benz, with her sons Eugen, 15, and Richard, 13, drove Karl Benz's Patent-Motorwagen from Mannheim to Pforzheim without his knowledge, about 60 miles (96.6 km) of unpaved roads in roughly 13 hours by Britannica's account, first long-distance automobile journey; other accounts give 106 km. Her stated purpose was visiting her mother, while Karl struggled to market his invention. She bought ligroin, petroleum solvent its engine burned, from a chemist in Wiesloch, since fuels were sold only by pharmacies; she cleared a blocked fuel pipe with her hat pin, fixed its ignition with her garter, and on returning had a cobbler fit leather to worn brake blocks, inventing brake linings.

ethiopia-rinderpest-famine-1888.summary: In 1887 cattle shipped from India to supply Italian troops at Massawa carried rinderpest, a viral disease unknown in Ethiopia. It swept through Tigray, Begemder, Gojjam and Shewa in 1888, killing most oxen and cattle, so fields went unploughed and milk and meat vanished while drought and locusts followed. Richard Pankhurst's reassessment of chronicles, travellers' letters and mission records estimated that about a third of Ethiopia's people died between 1888 and 1892. Angelo Caglioti argues that Italian planners misread emptied highlands as land open for settlers, a mirage that ended at Adwa in 1896. This panzootic then moved south, reaching Zambezi by 1896 and Cape Colony by 1897.

Rinderpest reshaped African pastoral economies for a generation and was declared eradicated worldwide in 2011.

kodak-camera-1888.summary: In 1888 Eastman's Kodak came loaded with film and was mailed back for developing: you press the button, we do the rest. It cost $25, came pre-loaded with a 100-exposure film roll, and could be mailed to Rochester with $10 for processing; it returned with prints, negatives and fresh film. By freeing photographers from complicated and expensive film development, it made photography more accessible than ever, met immediate public success, and launched a fad for amateur photography.

In 1885 he and William Walker patented first practical film roll holder, and his experiments led to an 1889 patent for nitrocellulose film. His Kodak was a box camera with fixed-focus lens and no viewfinder, aimed by two V-shaped silhouettes on top; it had a rotating key to advance film, a pull-string to set its shutter, and a button on its side to release it. Its slogan, "You Press the Button, We Do the Rest", entered common speech.

shallenberger-ac-meter-1888.summary: On 14 August 1888 Oliver B. Shallenberger, chief electrician at Westinghouse, receives US patent 388,003 for a Meter for Alternating Electric Currents. IEEE's history of him recounts the accident behind it: a spring fell into an arc lamp he was adjusting and began to rotate in its alternating field, and within weeks he had a disc meter that integrated current over time. Until then AC customers were charged a flat rate per lamp, so there was no reason to switch anything off. His meter made alternating current a saleable commodity midway through the war of the currents, and by 1900 Shallenberger meters were in use worldwide. Shallenberger retired in 1891 and died in 1898.

Shallenberger's electric meter borrowed that model and gave households their first continuous feedback on energy use, ancestor of today's smart meters. Westinghouse built the meter alongside Tesla's induction motor patents, bought in 1888; together they let alternating current drive machinery and be billed by use.

tesla-ac-motor-1888.summary: In May 1888 Nikola Tesla received US patents, filed from New York in late 1887, for motors running on alternating current, which travels far over wires and electrifies factories. He visualised a rotating magnetic field in Budapest and, posted to Strasbourg for Continental Edison in 1883, built his first induction motor after working hours (Britannica). Galileo Ferraris in Turin independently demonstrated a working model in 1885, and both designs needed no commutator, sliding contacts that wear in direct-current machines. That May George Westinghouse bought patent rights to Tesla's polyphase system of dynamos, transformers and motors, and Tesla presented his paper on alternating-current motors and transformers to the American Institute of Electrical Engineers; Westinghouse's first practical induction motor followed in 1892.

Turin's Royal Academy of Science published Ferraris's research in April 1888. Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky's cage-rotor motor of 1889 led to today's three-phase squirrel-cage design.

trans-caspian-railway-samarkand-1888.summary: General Mikhail Annenkov's railway battalions begin laying track eastward from Uzun-Ada on the Caspian in 1880 during Russia's campaign against Turkmen Geok-Tepe, extend it to Askhabad in 1885 and Merv in 1886, bridge the Amu Darya on a timber trestle more than two kilometres long in 1887, and open Samarkand station in May 1888. Across shifting Karakum dunes crews pinned sand with saxaul brush, clay and planted tamarisk, and water for locomotives came by tank car. About 1,400 kilometres of line let Russian troops, cotton and kerosene move in days instead of months by camel, and Bukhara's emirate acquired a Russian railway town, Kagan, at its gates. George Curzon rode it in 1888 and judged that it had changed Central Asia's strategic position more than any treaty; extensions reached Tashkent in 1899.

digboi-oil-assam-1889.summary: Railway builders of Assam Railways and Trading Company noticed oil on elephants' feet near Digboi in upper Assam and in 1889 drilled a well that struck oil at about 178 feet. Assam Oil Company formed in 1899 and commissioned a refinery at Digboi in 1901, earliest in Asia, processing crude from a field that worked continuously for over a century. Production stayed small by world standards, a few hundred barrels a day, yet Digboi trained Indian drillers and refiners, supplied kerosene to northeast India and became base for later Oil India exploration in Assam. It is still running, oldest producing oilfield in world.

Henry Villard, long-time Edison supporter and investor, proposed consolidating all of them, and Drexel, Morgan & Co., which had financed Edison's research, helped carry out that merger. In 1892 financier J. P. Morgan orchestrated its merger with Charles Coffin's Thomson-Houston Electric Company to form General Electric, without Edison, headquartered for many years at Schenectady; in 1896 GE was among the original twelve companies in Dow Jones Industrial Average.

eiffel-tower-1889.summary: In 1889 the Eiffel Tower opened at 300 metres, Earth's tallest structure, built in two years to show what engineers could do. In 1886 competition terms for its centrepiece required a 300-metre four-sided metal tower on Champ de Mars, which made Eiffel's selection inevitable, and Eiffel was to keep all income from it for 20 years. It remained world's tallest structure for 41 years, until New York's Chrysler Building in 1930, and is now recognised worldwide.

In May 1884 they sketched "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top"; architect Stephen Sauvestre added decorative arches and other embellishments. Prominent artists including Charles Garnier, Guy de Maupassant and Charles Gounod published their petition against it on 14 February 1887, two weeks after foundation work began. Its 18,038 pieces, made in Levallois-Perret, were joined with 2.5 million rivets. Structural work ended in March 1889.

french-panama-canal-failure-1889.summary: In 1889 France's Panama Canal company collapsed after 22,000 deaths from disease, that century's largest financial failure. Ferdinand de Lesseps's company had tried to build a canal across Panama, and its collapse became the nineteenth century's largest monetary corruption scandal. The United States bought its rights and property for $40 million under its Spooner Act of 1902, took possession on 4 May 1904 and opened its canal in 1914.

french-panama-canal-failure-1889.detail: Its court-appointed liquidator kept buildings, tools and machinery, but within a few years Panama's damp, warm climate caused heavy losses. France's government repeatedly delayed liquidation because American takeover offers seemed insufficient, and an 1890 inquiry recommended continuing as sluice canal and renewing its Colombian concession to 1904. By 1892 its scale was clear: some 800,000 French people, including 15,000 single women, had lost about 1.8 billion gold francs. Of 1.2 billion francs raised in nine issues, 960 million went to Panama, and much of what remained was pocketed by financiers and politicians. In 1892 and 1893, many members of parliament, including six ministers, were accused of taking bribes to hide its finances; Lesseps, his son Charles and engineer Gustave Eiffel received jail sentences, later annulled.

johnstown-flood-1889.summary: In May 1889 a neglected dam above Johnstown, Pennsylvania failed and 2,209 people died; the rich club that owned it paid nothing. Johnstown, Pennsylvania, lay 14 miles downstream. Momentarily dammed by debris at Conemaugh Viaduct, its surge rebuilt its head and struck downstream at 40 miles per hour and up to 60 feet high. In all it killed 2,208 people and caused US$17 million in damage. Clara Barton's American Red Cross mounted major relief, and this disaster later shaped American tort law's acceptance of strict liability.

hollerith-tabulator-census-1890.summary: In 1890 Hollerith's punch cards counted the US census in months rather than years; his firm became IBM. With America's Constitution requiring a census every ten years to apportion representatives and taxes, faster recording was needed. Hollerith, inspired by conductors who punched holes in railway tickets to record passengers' sex and approximate age, settled on cards with round holes in 12 rows and 24 columns, invented in the late 1880s.

Each card was then laid over pools of mercury; when wires were pressed down, holes let wires dip into mercury and close circuits, which drove electromechanical counters, sorted cards and rang a bell to confirm reading. His tabulator had 40 counters, each with a dial of 100 divisions. Some 100 million cards were generated and passed through his machines only four times. kitasato-tetanus-antitoxin-1890.detail: Kitasato, born in Higo Province, Japan, in 1853, was educated at Kumamoto Medical School and a predecessor of Tokyo Imperial University. He studied under Robert Koch at the University of Berlin from 1885 to 1891. Their work on tetanus and diphtheria founded serotherapy, treatment with antibody-bearing serum, which has benefited many worldwide; Behring received the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901 for it, while Kitasato, also nominated, did not. Kitasato returned to Japan in 1891, founded the Institute for Study of Infectious Diseases with Fukuzawa Yukichi's help, and in 1894 identified plague's bacterium in Hong Kong days before Alexandre Yersin found the same organism.

sherman-antitrust-act-1890.summary: In 1890 Congress's Sherman Act made monopolies illegal in the United States, a law later used to break up Standard Oil and AT&T. It prohibits anticompetitive agreements and monopolization or attempted monopolization. It was enacted in an era of "trusts" and "combinations" of businesses and capital organised to control markets by suppressing competition, whose monopolistic tendency had become public concern. Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States broke that company up by geography in 1911, and 1914's Clayton Act added practices it had missed.

It was first used on 6 August 1890 to execute William Kemmler at Auburn Prison, New York. This was one episode in the war of the currents: Thomas Edison's company sold low-voltage direct current for indoor lighting, and from 1886 George Westinghouse's company offered alternating current, which transformers could step down from high transmission voltage. That war ended when Edison Electric merged with Thomson-Houston as General Electric in 1892.

vucetich-fingerprints-1891.summary: Around 1891 Juan Vucetich, Croatian-born statistician in Buenos Aires provincial police, began filing fingerprints and devised a classification system he called dactyloscopy; Britannica places him in that force in 1888 and dates his system from then, while Mercedes García Ferrari (Historia Crítica, 2016) dates its creation to late nineteenth century. In 1892 a bloody print identified Francisca Rojas, who had killed her two children and cut her own throat to blame an outsider, among earliest criminal identifications by fingerprint. Argentine police adopted his method; García Ferrari shows how Latin American Scientific Congresses of 1901, 1905 and 1908 to 1909 legitimised it as Latin American science and spread it regionally, and it reached police forces in Europe and Asia. He published Dactiloscopía comparada in 1904, and his system remains in use in most Spanish-speaking countries.

In his design air was compressed inside its cylinder until hot, and fuel injected at that compression stroke's end ignited from its heat alone, with no spark plug; it was smaller and lighter than contemporary steam engines. His first successful engine, Motor 250/400, was officially tested in 1897 at 25 horsepower, and its fuel efficiency was measured at 75 percent above steam engines' theoretical 10 percent.

He knew that steam engines wasted as much as 90 percent of their fuel's energy and sought an internal combustion engine approaching the Carnot cycle's maximum theoretical efficiency. From 1893 to 1897 Heinrich von Buz, director of Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, let Diesel test and develop his ideas, with support from Krupp.

Morgan conceived and orchestrated this consolidation, with support from Drexel, Morgan & Co. and the Vanderbilt family. It was incorporated in New York and used its Schenectady plant as headquarters for many years; both merged companies' plants remained in operation under GE. In 1896 General Electric was among twelve original companies in the newly formed Dow Jones Industrial Average, where it remained, not continuously, for 122 years.

Government allotted irrigated squares to peasants recruited from central Punjab, founding Lyallpur (Faisalabad) on a grid plan. Nine canal colonies settled over two million hectares by 1930, making Punjab British India's granary and cotton supplier and supporting army recruitment. Perennial canals raised water tables and brought waterlogging and salinity within decades. This system, divided in 1947, became core of Pakistan's agriculture and object of Indus Waters Treaty.

Photography had reached Istanbul in 1839, and Pera studios run by Armenian, Greek and Levantine families supplied court portraits, tourist views and army documentation; these albums survive as a record of late Ottoman modernisation seen from his palace.

He patented hemispherical pearls, or mabes, in 1896, and in 1899 opened his first pearl shop in Tokyo's Ginza district, where staff explained cultured pearls to customers. Fully spherical pearls indistinguishable from finest natural ones took another twelve years, and commercially viable harvests came only in the 1920s.

yersin-plague-hong-kong-1894.summary: Plague from Yunnan reached Canton and then Hong Kong in spring 1894, killing thousands in Taipingshan district. Kitasato Shibasaburo's Japanese team, working from blood, announced findings days earlier but described an organism with inconsistent features. Yersin's report in Annales de l'Institut Pasteur, and later priority reviews, led to naming Yersinia pestis in 1970, and Yersin's Nha Trang laboratory produced early antiplague serum.

In 1897 he described his millimetre-wave research to London's Royal Institution: he used waveguides, horn antennas, dielectric lenses, polarisers and semiconductors at frequencies up to 60 GHz, and was first to use a semiconductor junction to detect radio waves.

He began his radio experiments in late 1894, when Marconi was developing wireless telegraphy and Popov his lightning detector. lumiere-cinematograph-1895.summary: On 28 December 1895 Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten short films to paying viewers in Salon Indien of the Grand Café on boulevard des Capucines, Paris, and cinema became public entertainment. Their Cinématographe, patented in 1895, served as camera, printer and projector, running perforated film at 16 frames per second. H. Mark Gosser (SMPTE Journal, 1996) calls it the first truly acceptable projection of film before a paying audience; earlier paid projections existed, since Max and Emil Skladanowsky had shown films to paying customers in Berlin with their Bioscop from 1 November 1895, and Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope of 1894 showed films to one viewer at a time through its peephole. Around 40 paying visitors attended, and Britannica marks this showing as cinema history's beginning.

roentgen-x-rays-1895.summary: In 1895 Röntgen discovered X-rays and photographed his wife Anna Bertha Ludwig's hand bones, first X-ray of a human body part. He submitted "On a new kind of ray: A preliminary communication" to Würzburg's Physical-Medical Society on 28 December 1895, first paper on X-rays. He received the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics.

roentgen-x-rays-1895.detail: Crookes tubes, invented around 1875, produced cathode rays, energetic electron beams, when high voltage ionised residual air inside them. From 1888 Philipp Lenard had built tubes with thin aluminium windows to see whether those rays could escape into air, and found that something came through that exposed photographic plates. Röntgen burned his lab notes before his death, but his biographers' likely reconstruction is that he had wrapped a Crookes tube in black cardboard to block its visible light and noticed faint green glow on a fluorescent screen painted with barium platinocyanide about a metre away; invisible rays were passing through the cardboard, and also through books and papers on his desk.

wells-time-machine-1895.summary: In 1895 Wells's The Time Machine imagined riding to AD 802,701 and finding humanity split by class into two species. Its protagonist, Victorian scientist known as the Time Traveller, journeys to that year and finds those species: fair, childlike Eloi and savage, simian Morlocks, distant descendants of his era's upper and lower classes.

battle-of-adwa-1896.summary: In March 1896 Ethiopia destroyed an Italian army at Adwa with modern rifles it had bought; an African state kept its independence by force. Italy had tried to force Ethiopia to accept its version of their Treaty of Wuchale, whose interpretation was disputed, and so impose a protectorate. Italy recognised Ethiopia's sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa, Francesco Crispi's government fell, and Ethiopia stayed independent until Italy's invasion forty years later, alone among African countries to owe its independence to a military victory.

battle-of-adwa-1896.detail: Menelik mobilised a massive army, estimated at 73,000 to over 100,000 men and mostly equipped with modern rifles imported from France and Russia. Baratieri's much smaller force was unfamiliar with the terrain and hampered by poor reconnaissance; under pressure from Rome to act decisively, he launched his surprise attack on Ethiopian forces camped near Adwa, advancing in separate columns through difficult ground, where they became isolated and were overwhelmed by coordinated Ethiopian assaults despite their artillery. Over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and around 3,800 captured; Ethiopian losses were 4,000 to 7,000 killed.

becquerel-radioactivity-1896.summary: In 1896 Becquerel found that uranium fogged photographic plates in the dark: atoms give off energy on their own. He thought phosphorescent materials might emit penetrating X-ray-like radiation when lit by bright sunlight, so through February he wrapped photographic plates and coins in thick black paper, laid phosphorescent uranium salts on top and set them in sun for hours. By May, after experiments with non-phosphorescent uranium salts, he concluded that penetrating radiation came from uranium without excitation by any external energy source.

becquerel-radioactivity-1896.detail: Becquerel, French experimental physicist, had long been interested in phosphorescence, emission of light of one colour after exposure to light of another. He had learned of Röntgen's X-rays when Henri Poincaré read Röntgen's paper to the French Academy of Sciences on 20 January. On 26 and 27 February skies were dark and overcast, so he left his layered plates in a dark cabinet, yet when developed object shadows were just as distinct as after sunlight. Intense research followed: thorium proved radioactive, and Marie and Pierre Curie found polonium and radium. Becquerel shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with the Curies.

marconi-radio-patent-1896.summary: In 1896 Marconi filed wireless telegraphy's first patent; messages could cross sea and sky without a wire. Wireless telegraphy had been tried before; no system had proved technically and commercially successful. His breakthrough came in summer 1895, when raising his antenna and grounding both transmitter and receiver, a technique borrowed from wired telegraphy, let signals carry about 2 km beyond Celestini hill. By March 1897 he had sent Morse signals about 3 miles across Salisbury Plain, and that year he founded The Wireless Telegraph & Signal Company.

Marconi, born in Bologna in 1874, had studied Hertz's work through physics professor Augusto Righi, and at 20 began experiments in his family's Villa Griffone attic, building a spark transmitter and a receiver using a coherer, an early detector whose resistance changed when radio waves struck it. Italy's Ministry of Post and Telegraphs never answered his request for funding, so in early 1896 he went to London with his mother, where William Preece, Chief Electrical Engineer of the General Post Office, backed him.

uganda-railway-1896.summary: In 1896 Britain began a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria; it cost 2,500 workers' lives and created Nairobi and Kenya's settler economy. It finished at its terminus, Kisumu on Lake Victoria's eastern shore, in 1901. In December 1890, months after Britain joined anti-slavery measures of the Brussels Conference Act, Britain's Foreign Office proposed a railway from Mombasa to Uganda to disrupt slave traffic from interior to coast; a bill introduced at Westminster in August 1895 became the Uganda Railway Act 1896. Its cost, estimated at £3 million to £5.5 million, and its casualties led critics to dub it Lunatic Line.

Some 200,000 rail lengths, 1.2 million sleepers and steel for viaducts had to be imported from India, which required a modern port at Kilindini Harbour. Construction relied heavily on labour from British India under extremely harsh conditions; several thousand Indian labourers died from disease, famine, accidents and wildlife, most famously two Tsavo lions that killed at least 28 workers in 1898.

In late December 1896 James Phillips of that protectorate had led 250 people toward Benin City to discuss trade, without waiting for Ovonramwen's approval to enter; Benin forces attacked them on 4 January and killed or captured almost everyone.

benin-expedition-1897-1897.detail: Benin had kept its independence through the Scramble for Africa, and its Oba's monopoly over trade in his territories was seen as a threat by the Royal Niger Company. In 1892 Vice-Consul Henry Gallwey pressed a treaty on a hesitant Ovonramwen to open free passage of goods and develop palm oil. Rear-Admiral Harry Rawson then invaded with 1,200 men. After Benin City fell, houses, sacred sites and palaces were looted and burned, including Ovonramwen's palace on 21 February. Some 2,500 artefacts went to Britain; about 40 percent entered British Museum collections, and Britain's Admiralty auctioned others from May 1897 to defray expedition costs. braun-cathode-ray-tube-1897.summary: In 1897 Ferdinand Braun built a cathode-ray tube, a glass screen painted by an electron beam; it became television's screen. His cold-cathode diode was a Crookes tube modified with a phosphor-coated screen that glowed where electrons struck it. In cathode-ray tubes, electron guns fire beams that deflection coils or plates steer and an anode accelerates toward that screen, drawing images such as oscilloscope waveforms or television frames.

In 1908 Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton described in Nature how "distant electric vision" could use Braun tubes as both transmitter and receiver. Western Electric's John Johnson and Harry Weinhart made the first hot-cathode tube, sold commercially from 1922, and Telefunken built the first commercial electronic television sets with cathode-ray tubes in Germany in 1934.

All four were Protestant Christians trained at American Presbyterian Mission Press, and they began by publishing books such as Bibles once financial backing arrived. From 1903 Zhang Yuanji, responding to China's move toward a new curriculum, created textbook and translation series, and from 1904 he launched popular periodicals including Dongfang Zazhi and Short Story Magazine.

Its headquarters moved to Beijing in 1954, and it continues today as a publisher of dictionaries, textbooks and Chinese language materials.

eijkman-beriberi-batavia-1897.summary: At a military medical laboratory in Batavia (Jakarta), Christiaan Eijkman noticed in 1889 that laboratory chickens fed cooked polished rice from hospital kitchen developed a nerve disorder resembling beriberi and recovered when fed unpolished rice. Through 1890s he and Gerrit Grijns ran feeding trials and prison surveys across Java showing that rice with its silver skin protected against beriberi, publishing a summary paper in 1897. Eijkman first proposed a toxin countered by a substance in bran; Grijns reframed it in 1901 as a dietary deficiency. Their work opened a path to vitamin B1, isolated from rice bran by Jansen and Donath in Batavia in 1926.

haffkine-plague-vaccine-bombay-1897.summary: When plague reached Bombay in 1896, Ukrainian-born bacteriologist Waldemar Haffkine, already known for a cholera vaccine tested in Calcutta, set up a laboratory in a corridor of Grant Medical College and grew Yersinia pestis in broth, killing that culture with heat. On 10 January 1897 he injected himself with 10 ml and ran a fever for days. Weeks later, during an outbreak in the Byculla House of Correction, he inoculated 147 prisoners who volunteered; among them two cases and no deaths followed, against twelve cases and six deaths among 172 who refused. The Government of India founded a Plague Research Laboratory under him, later the Haffkine Institute, which issued about 26 million doses across India between 1897 and 1925.

maidstone-chlorination-1897.summary: Typhoid broke out in Maidstone, Kent, in August 1897 after hop-pickers contaminated springs feeding Maidstone's supply. By 9 October there were 1,200 cases; its final count was 1,847 cases and 132 deaths in a town of 34,000. On 20 September suspect Tutsham springs were cut off, and on 16 October pathologist German Sims Woodhead supervised dosing of Barming reservoir and mains with chloride of lime, about ten tons in 200,000 gallons, flushed through overnight. It was an emergency disinfection rather than continuous treatment, but it is the earliest documented chlorination of a public supply. Continuous chlorination began at Lincoln in 1905 after another typhoid outbreak and at Jersey City in 1908, where it survived a court challenge and spread across America.

Isaacs then led it into radio broadcasting, where it was dominant in forming the British Broadcasting Company, while Marconi focused on research.

marconi-company-1897.detail: It founded American Marconi in 1899 and became Marconi's Wireless Telegraph Company in 1900. That year it set up Marconi International Marine Communication Company, and a training college followed in 1901. It sent transatlantic broadcasts between Clifden, Ireland, and Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, from 17 October 1907. When its finances faltered Marconi recruited Godfrey Isaacs as managing director, who turned it around and rode demand for maritime wireless after the Titanic sank in 1912; that year it moved to larger New Street Works in Chelmsford. It became one of Britain's most successful manufacturing companies.

ross-malaria-mosquito-1897.summary: Ronald Ross, an Indian Medical Service surgeon working in a tin-roofed hospital room in Secunderabad, had spent two years dissecting mosquitoes fed on malaria patients without result. On 20 August 1897 he examined "dapple-winged" mosquitoes (Anopheles) fed four days earlier on his patient Husein Khan and found pigmented cells in their stomach walls, the parasite's oocysts; a day later they had grown. He wrote in his Nobel lecture, "I counted altogether twelve of these cells in the insect." His paper appeared in the British Medical Journal on 18 December 1897. Transferred to Calcutta, he traced malaria's full cycle in birds in 1898, and Giovanni Grassi's team in Rome showed human transmission by Anopheles that same year. Ross received his Nobel Prize in 1902, and malaria control turned to draining, screening and killing mosquitoes.

thomson-electron-1897.summary: In 1897 J J Thomson found electrons, particles 1,000 times lighter than an atom and present in all matter: atoms had parts. Cathode rays were glowing beams seen in evacuated glass discharge tubes, then also called Lenard rays, and their nature was disputed; earlier investigators such as Heinrich Hertz had thought they could not be deflected electrically. He concluded that they were very light, negatively charged particles which were a universal building block of atoms, so atoms were divisible.

thomson-electron-1897.detail: Thomson found that they travelled much farther through air than expected for anything atom-sized. He estimated their mass by measuring heat generated when rays hit a thermal junction and comparing it with their magnetic deflection; his experiments suggested that they were over 1,000 times lighter than hydrogen atoms, and that their mass was the same whichever type of atom they came from. One month later he could reliably deflect them with an electric field by evacuating his tube to very low pressure. He called them corpuscles; later scientists preferred electron, a name George Johnstone Stoney had suggested in 1891. Thomson received the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics for his investigations of electrical conduction in gases.

curie-radium-polonium-1898.summary: In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie announced two new elements, polonium and radium, and Marie coined radioactivity. Using an electrometer, Pierre's sensitive device for measuring electric charge, she showed that pitchblende, a uranium mineral, was four times as active as pure uranium, so it must contain an element far more active.

curie-radium-polonium-1898.detail: Henri Becquerel had found in 1896 that uranium salts emitted rays, and Marie chose uranium rays as her thesis topic. They worked in a converted shed next to ESPCI that was poorly ventilated and not waterproof. Radium was elusive because it is chemically close to barium, which pitchblende also contains; from a tonne of ore they separated one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride in 1902, and Marie isolated pure radium metal in 1910. They shared 1903's Nobel Prize in Physics with Becquerel, and she won 1911's Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering and isolating these elements, the only person so far to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences.

garden-cities-1898.summary: In 1898 Ebenezer Howard proposed garden cities, planned towns of 32,000 ringed by farmland; suburbs and new towns worldwide follow his plan. He envisioned each garden city as a "third magnet" drawing residents and small businesses away from both too-crowded cities and too-isolated countryside. Howard founded the Garden City Association, later the Town and Country Planning Association, which created First Garden City Ltd in 1899 to build Letchworth, 34 miles outside London; Raymond Unwin and Barry Parker won its 1904 planning competition.

garden-cities-1898.detail: It was reissued in 1902 as "Garden Cities of To-morrow". Howard drew on Edward Bellamy's utopian novel Looking Backward and Henry George's Progress and Poverty. His idealised city housed 32,000 people on 9,000 acres, laid out in his diagrams in concentric rings with open spaces, public parks and six radial boulevards 120 feet wide, and clusters of such cities would orbit a central city of 58,000 people, linked by road and rail and separated by green belts. Howard bought land at Welwyn for his second garden city in 1919. The movement's emphasis on planning fed Britain's post-war New Towns Act, and garden cities inspired by his model have since been built all over the world.

war-of-the-worlds-1898.summary: In 1898 Wells's The War of the Worlds turned invasion by a superior technology against Britain, which practised it. Its unnamed narrator in Surrey, and his younger brother who flees to Essex, watch Martians invade London and southern England; their home planet has reached its "last stage of exhaustion", and they land on Horsell Common and lay waste to Woking with three-legged fighting machines armed with heat rays and toxic smoke.

war-of-the-worlds-1898.detail: Earthly bacteria, to which Martians had no immunity, save humanity where its armies fail. Wells, who had trained in biology, later said his inspiration was European colonisation's catastrophic effect on Aboriginal Tasmanians, and its plot has been read as commentary on evolution, imperialism and Victorian-era fears. It has never been out of print, is among science fiction's most discussed works, and is credited with establishing themes such as first contact and war between planets. Orson Welles's 1938 radio adaptation convinced part of its audience that a Martian invasion was under way.

aspirin-bayer-1899.summary: In 1899 Bayer began selling aspirin worldwide, the first mass-market synthetic drug. In 1897 Bayer scientists began studying it as a less-irritating replacement for common salicylate medicines, and Felix Hoffmann, or perhaps Arthur Eichengrün, first produced it in pure, stable form that year. Aspirin's popularity grew through the twentieth century's first half; Bayer lost its trademark in America and some other countries between 1918 and 1921 after letting other manufacturers use its name for years, so aspirin became a genericised trademark.

Sneader's account supports Eichengrün's claim and casts doubt on Hoffmann's credit. That BMJ page was access-gated, but its evidence reports these dates and finding.
aspirin-bayer-1899.detail: Salicin from willow bark, which human guts turn into salicylic acid, had been used for its health effects for at least 2,400 years. Charles Frédéric Gerhardt first made acetylsalicylic acid in 1853 by treating sodium salicylate with acetyl chloride. Its name blends a(cetyl) with spir, from Spirsäure, German for meadowsweet, from which salicylic acid was first isolated, plus drug suffix -in. Paracetamol in 1956 and ibuprofen in 1962 cut into its use, but John Vane showed in 1971 that it suppresses prostaglandins, winning a Nobel Prize in 1982, and trials established its anti-clotting value. Some 40,000 tonnes are consumed each year.

bolivia-patino-tin-llallagua-1900.summary: In 1900 Cochabamba-born storekeeper Simón Iturri Patiño, who had taken over La Salvadora claim at Llallagua in 1897, struck an exceptionally rich tin vein. As silver prices fell and canned-food and tinplate industries grew, Bolivian mines around Oruro and Potosí shifted to cassiterite, and Antofagasta railway wagons carried concentrates to Chilean ports. Patiño bought out neighbouring companies, built mills at Catavi and Uncía, acquired smelters in England and by 1924 controlled a large part of world tin production. John Hillman's study shows Bolivian output rising from about 1,000 tonnes in 1890 to nearly 20,000 tonnes in 1900, making tin Bolivia's main export for five decades, until nationalisation in 1952.

Patiño moved to Europe in 1912 and his group controlled smelting in Liverpool and Arnhem. Their movement had emerged in 1898 and 1899, and their rebellion ended in 1901 after that foreign invasion.

sydney-plague-rat-campaign-1900.summary: Bubonic plague reached Sydney in January 1900 aboard ships from Noumea and Hong Kong. Chief Medical Officer John Ashburton Thompson, following Simond's new hypothesis, treated rats and their fleas rather than human contact as main vector, and organised bounties that killed more than 100,000 rats, cleansing gangs that demolished and limewashed waterfront slums, and quarantine at North Head for contacts. By August 1900 there had been 303 cases and 103 deaths. Thompson's 1900 reports in Public Health and later Lancet papers were among first epidemiological demonstrations that rat plague preceded human plague, influencing global practice. Barr argues that dirt and fear framed political action ahead of Federation.

His factory produced sulphuric acid, phosphates, tinctures and quinine preparations from local raw materials, and employed his students from Presidency College, where he had prepared mercurous nitrite in 1896. Ray saw chemical industry as swadeshi self-reliance and wrote A History of Hindu Chemistry to show Indian precedents. Bengal Chemicals grew into one of India's largest drug makers before independence and survives today as a public sector company.

In Ohio janitor James Murray Spangler filed his portable electric suction sweeper in 1907, granted in June 1908, and sold rights to his cousin's husband William Hoover. Testing Albert Calmette's single cobra antiserum, he showed that it failed against Bothrops and Crotalus bites and that serum had to match venom species. He issued anti-bothropic and anti-crotalic sera, created a polyvalent serum, and distributed them to coffee plantations in exchange for live snakes shipped by rail in wooden boxes. Butantan became a centre for herpetology and venom research and later made vaccines; its 1911 treatise A defesa contra o ophidismo spread his methods across the Americas.

cape-town-plague-ndabeni-1901.summary: Bubonic plague reached Cape Town in early 1901 after infected forage arrived from Argentina for British army horses during the South African War; a first suspect ship, the Kilburn, had been quarantined in March 1900. Under public health powers Cape Colony's government forced some 6,000 to 7,000 African dock and railway workers out of inner-city districts to a fenced location at Uitvlugt on the Cape Flats, later Ndabeni. Maynard Swanson called this a sanitation syndrome: medical language of contagion turned into urban segregation, a pattern repeated at Port Elizabeth and Durban. Myron Echenberg's comparative study of plague ports shows Cape Town as the case where disease control most directly produced racial residential law.

landsteiner-blood-groups-1901.summary: Karl Landsteiner, an assistant at Vienna University's pathological-anatomical institute, mixed serum and red cells from himself and five colleagues and found that some combinations clumped and others did not. In a 1901 paper in the Wiener klinische Wochenschrift he sorted samples into three groups, A, B and C (later O); his students Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli added rare group AB in 1902. Transfusion had been tried since the 1660s with frequent deaths. Reuben Ottenberg in New York performed the first transfusion with compatibility testing in 1907 and showed by 1911 that typed transfusions were safe. Landsteiner received his Nobel Prize in 1930, and typing made 1930s blood banks and Second World War plasma programmes possible.

No recording was made and historians still debate whether he heard it; official wireless messages crossed the Atlantic between Poldhu and Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, in December 1902.

His will left 94% of his estate to fund prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. Inaugural laureates included Wilhelm Röntgen, Jacobus van ’t Hoff, Sully Prudhomme, Emil von Behring, and Jean Henri Dunant and Frédéric Passy, who shared the Peace Prize.

Drawn from animal glands, it became medicine's first effective drug for opening asthma sufferers' airways.

Investors' money went instead to Marconi's cheaper working system; Wardenclyffe's 187-foot tower was never completed as planned, operations closed in 1905, and it was demolished for scrap in 1917 to cover Tesla's debts.

yawata-steel-works-1901.summary: In 1901 Japan lit its first modern blast furnace at Yahata; within decades it made steel for its ships, rails and guns. Its state-owned Imperial Steel Works had been set up in 1896 to feed growing shipbuilding, railway, construction and armaments industries. Poor output, high coke consumption and other failures led to suspension the following year; Japanese engineers, among them metallurgist Kageyoshi Noro, fixed those defects, and by 1912 Yahata made 80% of Japan's pig iron.

Its gates opened each year to pass flood and sediment, storing no water from year to year; found too small for Egypt's needs, it was raised in 1907-1912 and 1929-1933 and later fitted to generate electricity.

It answered a problem at Sackett-Wilhelms Lithographing & Publishing Company in Brooklyn, where humid summer air made paper expand and shrink and spoiled color printing. Carrier patented his spray-type apparatus in 1906 and founded Carrier Corporation in 1915.

pacific-cable-1902.summary: On 31 October 1902, cable ship Anglia spliced last section of a 12,900-kilometre telegraph cable linking Bamfield on Vancouver Island to Fanning Island, Suva, Norfolk Island and then Southport in Queensland and Doubtless Bay in New Zealand. Owned jointly by British, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand governments through Pacific Cable Board, it broke Eastern Extension Company's monopoly on Australasian traffic and completed an 'All Red Line' touching only British territory. Fanning to Bamfield section of 6,000 kilometres was longest single cable yet laid. Boyce's 2000 study traces two decades of lobbying by Sandford Fleming and colonial governments against Treasury and Eastern Extension resistance.

philippines-cholera-1902.summary: Cholera arrived in Manila in March 1902, at close of Philippine-American War, and spread through provinces for two years. American military and civil health officers under Dean Worcester quarantined districts, burned Farola and other Manila neighbourhoods, banned sale of fresh vegetables and detained suspected carriers, measures that Filipinos often evaded or resisted. Ken De Bevoise estimates deaths at roughly 200,000 in 1902-1904, atop losses from war and famine. Warwick Anderson reads this campaign as a founding moment for American colonial medicine in Asia, with laboratories, sanitary codes and later Culion leper colony following from it.

baghdad-railway-concession-1903.summary: On 5 March 1903 Abdülhamid II's government signs a convention with Deutsche Bank's Anatolian Railway Company, led by Arthur von Gwinner, for a line from Konya through Taurus and Amanus ranges to Mosul, Baghdad and Basra, with kilometric revenue guarantees and rights to minerals and antiquities along its route. British and Russian objections turned financing into a decade of diplomacy; German crews reached Bulgurlu in 1904, tunnelled Taurus passes during World War I and used unfinished track to move troops, and in 1915 Armenian deportees were marched along it. Turkish, French and Iraqi successors completed remaining gaps, and a through train first ran from Istanbul to Baghdad in July 1940. Ottoman engineers trained on this project, and its alignment fixed routes of modern Turkish, Syrian and Iraqi railways.

Lady Forrest started pumping machinery at Pumping Station Number One on January 22, 1903, and water flowed into Mount Charlotte Reservoir on January 24. Designer C. Y. O'Connor, derided in parliament and press as attempting the impossible, had died by suicide less than 12 months earlier; it still supplies more than 100,000 people.

Between 1897 and 1906, 4,000 European immigrants had died of yellow fever in Rio. In 1904 he proposed restoring compulsory smallpox vaccination, and popular resistance helped trigger the Vaccine Revolt; in 1907 Berlin's International Congress on Hygiene and Demography awarded him its gold medal for Rio's sanitation.

uganda-sleeping-sickness-1903.summary: From 1901 sleeping sickness spread along Lake Victoria's northern shore in Busoga and Buganda, killing well over 250,000 people within a decade as colonial transport, resettlement and ecological change brought people into tsetse habitat. A Royal Society commission reached Entebbe in 1902. On 12 November 1902 Aldo Castellani saw a living trypanosome in cerebrospinal fluid drawn by lumbar puncture from a patient, and reported further cases in early 1903. David Bruce, arriving in March 1903, confirmed the parasite's role and tsetse transmission, after which Uganda cleared lakeshore populations inland. Maryinez Lyons places this outbreak in the wider colonial disease history of Central Africa.

Robert Harms's study of ABIR shows how wild-rubber vines were exhausted by 1906, breaking the system. His report fuelled E. D. Morel's Congo Reform Association and Belgium's annexation of Leopold II's colony in 1908.

Gillette, a travelling salesman for Crown Cork, had his idea in 1895; MIT-trained engineer William Nickerson worked out how to harden and sharpen steel that thin, and American Safety Razor Company, founded 1901, began production in 1903. His blade made shaving a home task rather than a barber's trade and set a pattern of selling a cheap holder and a stream of consumable blades, later copied from ink cartridges to coffee pods. nagaoka-saturnian-atom-1904.summary: In papers read to Tokyo Mathematico-Physical Society in December 1903 and published in Philosophical Magazine and Nature in 1904, Hantaro Nagaoka of Tokyo Imperial University modelled an atom as a large positive central mass circled by rings of electrons, by analogy with Maxwell's analysis of Saturn's rings. He used it to discuss spectral lines and radioactivity, in contrast to J. J. Thomson's model of electrons embedded in a diffuse positive sphere. Instability of such rings under electrostatic repulsion drew criticism and Nagaoka dropped it by 1908, yet Ernest Rutherford cited Nagaoka's paper in his 1911 article proposing a nuclear atom from alpha-scattering results.

Smallpox, bubonic plague and yellow fever were ravaging Brazil's capital. Rioters also drew on anger at public services and mayor Pereira Passos's urban reforms; 30 people were killed, 110 wounded, and 945 arrested, and on 16 November the government declared a state of emergency and suspended mandatory vaccination.

Zhan had been educated in the United States. He laid a zigzag section near Qinglongqiao station to climb steep mountain grades and finished two years ahead of schedule and under budget, giving China its first railway built without foreign help.

broken-hill-froth-flotation-1905.summary: Broken Hill's silver-lead-zinc lode left mountains of tailings holding about 20 percent zinc that gravity separation could not recover. Between 1901 and 1905 Melbourne brewer Charles Potter and Broken Hill Proprietary's general manager Guillaume Delprat patented processes in which finely ground ore, hot acidulated water and gas bubbles lifted sulphide minerals into a froth that could be skimmed. BHP's plant ran from 1903; a 1905 Victorian Supreme Court case, Potter v BHP, fought over priority and ended in a combined Potter-Delprat name. Rival inventors including Minerals Separation's agitation-froth process soon followed. Flotation became standard worldwide for sulphide ores and today processes billions of tonnes of ore a year.

Lyster's 1912 selective flotation and xanthate collectors in 1925 completed modern technique. A 1918 review recorded a decade of practice. Zinc recovered from tailings supported smelters at Port Pirie and Risdon and Australia's role in First World War metal supply. Flotation chemistry drew on Haynes's 1860 oil patent and Elmore's 1898 bulk-oil process.

michell-thrust-bearing-1905.summary: Melbourne engineer Anthony George Maldon Michell solved Reynolds's lubrication equations for a sliding pad in 1905 and designed a thrust bearing whose segmental pads pivot to form a wedge of oil film, carrying loads many times those of older collar bearings with far less friction. His British patent 875 of 16 January 1905 and Australian patents followed. First installation ran a centrifugal pump at Cohuna on Murray River in 1907. Royal Navy adopted Michell bearings for propeller shafts during First World War, saving space and power; hydro and steam turbines worldwide followed. Cherry's Royal Society memoir calls it an invention that made large propeller drives and turbines possible.

Michell also invented a crankless engine (1920s) and wrote a lubrication textbook. He worked as a consulting engineer on irrigation and hydraulic schemes in Victoria. Bearing design still follows his analysis, with tilting pads in hydroelectric turbines and ship propeller shafts carrying thousands of tonnes.

necaxa-hydroelectric-plant-1905.summary: In December 1905 Mexican Light and Power Company, a Canadian-registered firm engineered by Frederick Stark Pearson, began generating at Necaxa in Puebla's Sierra Norte, where dams on Necaxa and Tenango rivers fed water through tunnels and penstocks dropping more than 400 metres to turbines. Transmission lines at 60,000 volts, then among Earth's longest and highest-voltage, carried power 150 kilometres to Mexico City's trams, lights and factories and to silver mines at El Oro and Pachuca. Capacity reached about 100 megawatts by 1910, and its earth-fill dams were among those of greatest volume yet built. Necaxa supplied most of central Mexico's electricity for three decades and remains in service.

His claim has not been well documented. His proven firsts include transmitting speech by radio in 1900 and, in January 1906, two-way Morse exchange across the Atlantic, between his station at Brant Rock, Massachusetts, and Machrihanish, Scotland.

nauru-phosphate-mining-1906.summary: Albert Ellis identified a doorstop in Sydney as high-grade phosphate rock in 1899 and traced it to Nauru and Banaba (Ocean Island). Under German colonial rule, Pacific Phosphate Company began shipping Nauru rock in 1906 and 1907. After 1920 British Phosphate Commissioners for Britain, Australia and New Zealand took over, selling phosphate below world prices to farmers at home while paying Nauruans tiny royalties. Superphosphate from Nauru underpinned Australian wheat and New Zealand pasture through 1960s. Mining removed topsoil and left coral pinnacles across 80 percent of island. Nauru gained independence in 1968, bought the industry in 1970 and in 1989 sued Australia at International Court of Justice over rehabilitation.

Its walls are sun-baked earth bricks and sand with earth-based mortar.

German liners had held it since 1897, so Britain's government lent Cunard £2,600,000 to build her and Lusitania at a guaranteed 24-knot service speed. On her return crossing of 30 November to 5 December she took the eastbound Blue Riband at 23.69 knots; she added a westbound record in September 1909 and held both until 1929.

Within a week Knickerbocker Trust Company, New York City's third-largest trust, failed, and stocks fell almost 50% from their 1906 peak. J. P. Morgan pledged his own money and rallied other bankers to shore up banking, which exposed how little cash Washington's Treasury could supply in a panic; Congress passed its Aldrich-Vreeland Act in May 1908 and, after its National Monetary Commission reported, the Federal Reserve Act in December 1913.

Early calculations of its own weight had never been rechecked once design was finished, and distortions in key members seen that summer went unheeded. A Royal Commission inquiry followed; in 1916 its redesigned successor dropped its central span into the river, killing 13 more, and opened in 1917 with a 549-metre cantilever span that remains unmatched in length.

William Knox D'Arcy had bought a 60-year concession from Shah Mozaffar al-Din in 1901 and, deep in debt after years without a find, saw his interests taken over by a Burmah Oil syndicate in 1905. Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later BP, was founded in 1909 and by 1912 had piped Masjed Soleyman's oil to a refinery at Abadan, shipping its first cargo that March.

ford-model-t-1908.summary: In 1908 Ford's Model T went on sale, the first car ordinary families could afford. Its low price came partly from moving assembly lines with fully interchangeable parts, which cut build time from 12½ hours to 93 minutes by 1914; its Runabout fell from $825 in 1909 to $260 by 1925. Ford built 15 million, and by its ten-millionth, half of all cars worldwide were Model Ts.

hejaz-railway-1908.summary: In September 1908 the Hejaz Railway reached Medina, 1,300 kilometres from Damascus; pilgrimage time fell from 40 days to five. Sultan Abdul Hamid II had planned it to carry pilgrims toward Mecca and bind distant Arab provinces to Istanbul; World War I stopped it 400 kilometres short of Mecca, and during the Arab Revolt guerrillas led by T. E. Lawrence ambushed its trains.

ikeda-umami-msg-1908.summary: In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kelp and named its taste umami. Umami now counts among five basic tastes with sweet, sour, bitter and salty. He had noticed in 1907 that his family's dashi tasted better with kombu in it. By 1909 he had patented a process for mass-producing monosodium glutamate from wheat and soybeans, sold as Ajinomoto, 'essence of flavor'.

jersey-city-chlorination-1908.summary: In 1908 Jersey City became the first American city to chlorinate its drinking water. Dilute chloride of lime at 0.2 to 0.35 parts per million killed bacteria that spread typhoid, cholera and dysentery. John L. Leal conceived it and George Warren Fuller designed its plant; within a few years chlorine disinfection spread to drinking water systems worldwide.

thor-electric-washing-machine-1908.summary: Hurley Machine Company of Chicago puts its Thor on sale, a galvanised drum turned by an electric motor, which IEEE's engineering timeline lists as America's first commercially sold electric washer, in 1907. Hurley engineer Alva J. Fisher filed its drive mechanism on 27 May 1909 and received US patent 966,677 on 9 August 1910. Britannica notes that manually controlled electric washers reached a wide market in the 1920s and that the first automatic machine, a front loader cycling through wash, drain, rinse and spin without attention, appeared in 1937. Ruth Schwartz Cowan later argued such machines raised standards of cleanliness more than they cut hours women spent on laundry.

He won Daily Mail's £1,000 prize for crossing by heavier-than-air aircraft. Some 10,000 people had gathered at Calais; he landed heavily in Northfall Meadow beside Dover Castle, breaking a propeller blade and damaging his undercarriage, but walked away unhurt and famous.

chagas-disease-1909.summary: Sent in 1907 by Instituto Oswaldo Cruz to control malaria among workers extending the Central Railway at Lassance, Minas Gerais, Carlos Chagas worked from a railway carriage. Railway engineers showed him blood-sucking barbeiro bugs that infested mud-walled houses; in December 1908 he found a flagellate protozoan in their gut and named it Trypanosoma cruzi after his mentor. On 14 April 1909 he found the same parasite in the blood of a feverish two-year-old girl, Berenice. His 1909 paper in Memorias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz described agent, vector, human disease and reservoir animals in one stroke, a feat without parallel in parasitology. Chagas disease still infects an estimated six to seven million people, mostly in Latin America.

forster-machine-stops-1909.summary: In 1909 E M Forster's The Machine Stops imagined people alone in cells, talking through screens, fed by a machine they worship. Humanity lives underground, each person in one cell, served by a giant Machine that provides everything and that people come to worship, until it fails and their society collapses with it. Forster wrote it to rebut H. G. Wells's A Modern Utopia of 1905, blaming technology rather than politics as humanity's controlling force; readers have since found instant messaging, social media and the Internet in it.

futurist-manifesto-1909.summary: In 1909 Marinetti's Futurist Manifesto declared a racing car more beautiful than classical sculpture: art embraced its machine age. It launched an avant-garde movement founded in Milan that praised speed, technology, youth and violence, glorified objects such as cars, airplanes and industrial cities, and scorned museums and the past. Painters Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Luigi Russolo and others soon joined, and Futurists went on to issue manifestos on painting, architecture, music, cinema, fashion and cuisine.

haber-ammonia-1909-1909.summary: In 1909 Fritz Haber made ammonia from the nitrogen in air, the process behind fertiliser that feeds half of us. His assistant Robert Le Rossignol and he demonstrated it at laboratory scale that summer, producing ammonia drop by drop at about 125 mL per hour. Ammonia is nitrogen fertilizer's base; Carl Bosch scaled their process up for BASF, whose Oppau plant began industrial production in 1913.

Jamsetji Tata had planned a research institute to advance India's scientific capabilities since meeting Swami Vivekananda on a ship in 1893; Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV gave about 371 acres of land and Tata gave buildings. Morris Travers, co-discoverer of the noble gases, became its first director, and its first students were admitted on 24 July 1911.

Paul Ehrlich had theorized that screening many compounds would turn up one that killed microbes without killing their host; his lab synthesized arsphenamine in 1907, and Sahachiro Hata found its effect on syphilis in 1909 while testing hundreds of arsenic compounds. Easier-to-prepare Neosalvarsan followed in 1912.

baro-kano-railway-1911.summary: Northern Nigeria's government built a 3 ft 6 in gauge line from Baro on Niger's bank to Kano, authorised in August 1907 and laid largely by Nigerian labour, about 15,000 workers at peak in early 1910. Railhead reached Zaria in January 1911 and Kano on 28 March 1911, 366 miles from Baro, at roughly £3,500 a mile. British planners expected cotton; instead Hausa farmers and Kano merchants shipped groundnuts, whose exports leapt from a few thousand tons to a cash crop that defined northern Nigeria's economy, as Jan Hogendorn documented. This line linked Kano's old caravan trade to Lagos and Atlantic shipping.

At 4.2 K he observed its resistance abruptly disappear. An ordinary metal's resistance falls gradually as it cools; a superconductor's drops to exactly zero, and it expels magnetic fields, behavior only quantum mechanics could later explain.

Thomson's plum pudding model, with positive charge spread through whole atoms, could explain. That central region was later known as the atomic nucleus, though Rutherford did not use that term in his paper.

Taylor, a mechanical engineer and former manufacturing manager, was by then consulting for industry; in 2001 the Academy of Management's Fellows voted it first among twentieth-century management books.

Exit doors had been locked to stop unauthorized breaks and theft, no sprinklers existed, and one flimsy fire escape collapsed, so many workers jumped from windows. wu-lien-teh-manchurian-plague-1911.summary: Pneumonic plague spread from marmot hunters in Transbaikalia along new railways to Harbin in autumn 1910 and killed some 60,000 people across Manchuria within months. Qing government sent Wu Lien-teh, a Penang-born, Cambridge-trained physician, who performed an autopsy, identified airborne spread between people and ordered gauze-and-cotton masks for staff and public, isolation wagons, travel controls and, with imperial permission, cremation of frozen corpses in January 1911. Deaths ended by April. Wu chaired International Plague Conference in Mukden that year and led a Manchurian Plague Prevention Service until 1931. Christos Lynteris's study traces how Wu's mask became a template for epidemic protective equipment.

abadan-refinery-opens-1912.summary: After oil was struck at Masjed Soleyman in May 1908, Anglo-Persian Oil Company leased a square mile of Abadan island from Shaikh Khazal of Mohammerah in 1909 and shipped sixty miles of six-inch pipe from America to carry crude down to tidewater. Indian fitters and clerks, Chinese carpenters and Arab and Persian labourers built stills and tanks beside the Shatt al-Arab, and refining began in 1912 at about 2,400 barrels a day, 120,000 tons a year, though early runs broke down and product quality was poor. Britain's Admiralty bought a controlling stake in 1914 to fuel its oil-burning fleet, and capacity rose to a million tons by 1918, five million by 1930 and ten million by 1939, making Abadan the largest refinery anywhere and a company town of segregated bungalows and workers' lines whose strikes shaped Iranian politics.

radio-act-1912-1912.summary: In 1912 America required licences for radio transmitters. US radio had gone largely unregulated since the late 1890s, even after 1906's Berlin convention called for licensing; Titanic's sinking that April gave licensing new urgency. Radio then meant point-to-point maritime, transoceanic and amateur stations, and it proved inadequate once public broadcasting began.

titanic-sinking-1912.summary: In April 1912 the Titanic, called unsinkable, hit an iceberg and 1,500 died for want of lifeboats; maritime law changed within two years. Watertight compartments and remotely closed watertight doors had given the White Star liner its 'unsinkable' reputation; under accepted practice, which treated lifeboats as ferries to nearby rescue ships, it carried boats for only about half of those aboard.

torres-quevedo-ajedrecista-1912.summary: In 1912 Leonardo Torres Quevedo built a machine that played a chess endgame against any human and won, with no hidden operator. It played a simplified endgame of white king and rook against black king, enforcing its rules mechanically and electromechanically with no hidden human, unlike earlier so-called automatons such as the Mechanical Turk. First demonstrated in 1913 and exhibited in Paris in 1914, it anticipated software chess programs by decades and was a precursor of computer chess.

wegener-continental-drift-1912.summary: In January 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that continents had once formed a single landmass, Pangaea, before breaking apart and drifting to their present locations; he expanded it into a book in 1915. Geologists largely rejected continental drift into the 1950s, partly because no plausible driving force was known; Wegener did not live to see it validated and absorbed into plate tectonics.

federal-reserve-act-1913.summary: In December 1913 America created the Federal Reserve, a central bank to stop bank panics that had recurred every generation. America had gone nearly 80 years without a central bank, and 1907's panic had persuaded many that banking and currency needed reform. Introduced by Wilson, Congressman Carter Glass and Senator Robert Latham Owen, it created the Federal Reserve System: twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks that manage money supply, lend to banks, oversee them and serve as lender of last resort, under a seven-member Federal Reserve Board.

ford-assembly-line-1913.summary: In 1913 Ford's moving assembly line cut car build time from 12½ hours to 93 minutes: mass production. Ford's William Klann had brought that idea back from Swift & Company's Chicago slaughterhouse, where carcasses moved along a conveyor past butchers who each repeated one cut. It divided assembly into 45 steps and kept evolving through time and motion study.

haber-bosch-1913.summary: In 1913 BASF began making ammonia from air at factory scale; fertiliser lifted limits on how many could eat. Carl Bosch had scaled up Fritz Haber's 1909 laboratory process, Bosch's team, Alwin Mittasch prominent in it, had found a cheap iron catalyst still used today, and the Oppau plant reached 20 tonnes a day in 1914. Its ammonia fed nitrogen fertiliser and, once the First World War cut Germany off from Chilean nitrate, explosives.

kingsbury-commitment-1913.summary: In 1913 AT&T agreed to connect rival phone companies and sell its Western Union stake to avoid being broken up: a regulated monopoly. Facing a government antitrust investigation, the company had spent months negotiating; president Theodore Vail wanted one unified telephone system, and its refusal to connect rivals to its long-distance network, by far the nation's finest, had alarmed regulators. The commitment came as a letter from Vice President Nathan Kingsbury and did not require AT&T to interconnect its local services with other local providers.

raja-harishchandra-phalke-1913.summary: Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, a trained lithographer and photographer, shot Raja Harishchandra over several months in Bombay and Nashik area and showed it at Coronation Cinematograph on 3 May 1913. He imported a Williamson camera and raw film from London, processed and printed footage himself and trained actors and technicians. Male actors played women's roles. He followed with Mohini Bhasmasur and Satyavan Savitri and set up Hindustan Film Company at Nashik in 1917. His choice of Puranic stories defined a mythological genre and his vertically integrated studio was template for Indian film industry, now largest in world by output.

ramanujan-hardy-letter-1913.summary: In 1913 a Madras clerk, Ramanujan, mailed Hardy pages of theorems; Hardy brought him to Cambridge, and his notebooks still yield results. Self-taught and working as a clerk in Madras, Ramanujan had failed to interest most professional mathematicians in results too novel and oddly presented for them. Hardy recognized his work as extraordinary and arranged for him to come to Cambridge; Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918, compiled nearly 3,900 results in his life, and died in India in 1920 aged 32.

activated-sludge-1914.summary: At Manchester Corporation's Davyhulme works, chemists Edward Ardern and William Lockett, under Gilbert Fowler, bubbled air through sewage in 80-ounce bottles in 1913 and, instead of discarding settled solids, kept them for each new batch. After five weeks of recycling, a batch cleared in 24 hours instead of weeks. On 3 April 1914 they read "Experiments on the oxidation of sewage without the aid of filters" to the Society of Chemical Industry at Manchester's Grand Hotel, naming those solids "activated sludge". Worcester built the first full plant in 1916 and Davyhulme ran one million gallons a day by 1921. Patents by Jones and Attwood slowed uptake in Britain while American cities such as Milwaukee adopted it; it remains standard at urban treatment plants worldwide.

agote-citrated-blood-transfusion-1914.summary: On 9 November 1914 Luis Agote, director of Instituto Modelo de Clínica Médica at Hospital Rawson in Buenos Aires, transfused 300 millilitres of blood mixed with sodium citrate from hospital porter Ramón Mosquera into a patient, with press photographers present. Citrate stopped clotting, so blood no longer had to pass directly from donor vein to recipient vein. Agote cabled his results to European governments at war and published them in Anales del Instituto Modelo in January 1915. Albert Hustin in Brussels had used citrate in March 1914 and Richard Lewisohn in New York set safe doses in 1915; Agote's demonstration drew publicity none of them had. Citrated, refrigerated blood made blood banks possible within two decades.

ford-five-dollar-day-1914.summary: In January 1914 Ford doubled his workers' pay to $5 a day; turnover fell and his workers could afford his cars. Ford said he meant to end turnover so heavy that some departments hired 300 men a year to fill 100 jobs, though Raff reads it as rent-sharing under union threat; the move proved profitable, forced Detroit competitors to raise wages, and came with conditions policed by a Social Department that frowned on drinking and gambling.

France had begun digging in 1881 and gone bankrupt in 1889 after engineering failures and an estimated 22,000 deaths from disease and accidents. America took over in 1904; Colonel William Gorgas's campaign against mosquitoes nearly eliminated yellow fever and malaria, though about 5,600 workers, mostly West Indian labourers, still died.

Anaconda Copper bought it in 1923, Chile nationalized its copper around 1971 and state company Codelco now runs what is described as the world’s largest open pit by excavated volume.

Chemist Fritz Haber had proposed heavier-than-air chlorine in place of tear gas and supervised installation of 5,730 cylinders. French troops in its path suffered 2,000 to 3,000 casualties and fled, opening a 6-kilometre gap in Allied lines, but German infantry dug in rather than advance on Ypres; Canadian troops identified chlorine by its smell and held their flank.

One design used electrostatics, another thin quartz crystals that vibrate under voltage, drawing on piezoelectricity, which Langevin's teacher Pierre Curie had found; each timed its signal's round trip to calculate submarine distance. An operational active system had been built by 1918, as World War I ended.

Britain and France had developed tanks separately to break trench warfare's deadlock on Europe's Western Front. Mark I grew from Little Willie, William Foster & Co.'s 1915 prototype built in Lincoln; for secrecy its hulls were described in shop orders as water carriers, hence tanks.

addis-djibouti-railway-1917.summary: In 1917 Djibouti's railway reached Addis Ababa after 20 years of building; Ethiopia had a link to the sea it did not own. Begun in 1897, a year after Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa, its single meter-gauge track stretched 784 km and replaced six weeks of camel and mule caravan from Djibouti. It gave landlocked Ethiopia its only access to the sea, and towns grew along its line as trade expanded.

fordson-tractor-1917.summary: Henry Ford and Son, organized 27 July 1917 in Dearborn, ships its first Fordson Model F tractor on 6 October 1917 against a British government order for 7,000 to replace horses and farmhands lost to war; 254 leave by year end and 6,000 plus 1,000 in parts by April 1918. Its frameless design uses engine and transmission castings as chassis, weighs about 1,230 kilograms and costs 750 dollars, falling to 395 dollars in a 1922 price war with International Harvester. Fordson number 100,000 rolls out on 21 February 1920; about 740,000 are built in the United States by 1928. Olmstead and Rhode's 2001 study finds tractor diffusion across American farms was more rapid than historians had thought, even as horses and tractors coexisted for decades.

Farmall of 1924 and Ferguson's three-point hitch answered those. Cork, Ireland production ran from 1919 and Soviet plants built licensed copies. Within three decades tractors freed cropland once devoted to feeding draft animals for food crops. Olmstead and Rhode count tractors replacing some 23 million draft animals in the United States by 1960.

radium-girls-1917.summary: From 1917 women painting watch dials with radium were told to lick their brushes; their deaths won workers the right to sue employers. They had been told to point their brushes on their lips, because rags or water rinses wasted time and paint, and that it was harmless. Workers in Illinois and Connecticut faced similar exposure in the 1920s; by 1927 more than 50 had died, five New Jersey women won a settlement in 1928, and their cases helped establish occupational disease labor law.

sundback-zipper-1917.summary: On 20 March 1917 Swedish-born engineer Gideon Sundback, working for Hookless Fastener Company in Meadville, Pennsylvania, receives US patent 1,219,881 for a Separable Fastener: rows of cupped metal teeth on cloth tapes that a slider meshes and parts. Whitcomb Judson had shown a clumsy clasp locker at Chicago's 1893 fair; Sundback's Hookless No. 2, on sale from 1914, stayed shut and could be made by machine, a first. US Army flying suits and money belts used it; B. F. Goodrich named it the zipper in 1923 for its rubber galoshes, and clothing adopted it in the 1930s. Sundback also designed machines that stamped and set its teeth.

spanish-flu-1918.summary: Between 1918 and 1920 influenza infected about 500 million people, a third of humanity, and killed between 17 million and 50 million by competing estimates, some running to 100 million. It was caused by an H1N1 subtype of influenza A and broke out as the First World War ended; wartime censors suppressed bad news while newspapers in neutral Spain reported freely, so it was misnamed Spanish flu. Unlike most influenza, it killed young adults at unusually high rates, with its deadliest wave from late August 1918.

Winston Churchill presented them Daily Mail's £10,000 prize for crossing in under 72 hours, and King George V knighted them a week later.

great-molasses-flood-1919.summary: In January 1919 a tank in Boston burst and a wave of molasses killed 21 people; the court case made companies answer for their engineering. Holding 2.3 million US gallons, about 13,000 short tons, it loosed a wave 25 feet high moving at an estimated 35 miles per hour; 21 people died and about 150 were injured. It had been poorly built, insufficiently tested and leaking since 1915. 119 residents brought one of Massachusetts' first class-action suits against owner United States Industrial Alcohol, which was found responsible, a milestone in modern corporate regulation.

scadta-colombia-airmail-1919.summary: On 5 December 1919 Colombian and German investors in Barranquilla founded Sociedad Colombo-Alemana de Transportes Aéreos. From 1920 its Junkers F 13 floatplanes, flown by German pilots such as Hellmuth von Krohn and managed by Austrian Peter Paul von Bauer, carried mail and passengers along Magdalena river between Barranquilla and Girardot, cutting a journey of a week or more by steamer to a few hours. SCADTA built its own airfields and radio stations, printed its own stamps under a government concession, and extended routes to Bogotá, Medellín and Ecuador. Pan American Airways secretly bought control in 1931; SCADTA merged into Avianca in 1940, and Avianca counts among airlines with longest continuous operation anywhere.

shu-zhendong-chinese-typewriter-1919.summary: Engineer Shu Zhendong, working at Commercial Press in Shanghai, refined a design by MIT-trained Zhou Houkun into a machine with a tray bed of about 2,500 common-usage characters in metal type, picked one at a time by a lever that lifted and struck each slug against paper. Commercial Press put Shu-style typewriters into production around 1919 and sold them to banks, government offices and newspapers through 1920s and 1930s. Thomas Mullaney's research shows how typists rearranged tray beds by frequency and adjacency, an early form of predictive text that continued under Maoist offices and anticipated input methods for Chinese computing.

argentina-radio-broadcast-parsifal-1920.summary: On 27 August 1920, after dark, Enrique Telémaco Susini, César Guerrico, Luis Romero Carranza and Miguel Mujica, medical students and radio amateurs later called 'los locos de la azotea', used a five-watt transmitter and a war-surplus Telefunken valve on Teatro Coliseo's roof to broadcast a performance of Parsifal to a few dozen receivers in Buenos Aires. They continued nightly with opera and concerts, forming Radio Argentina, and sold receivers through a company they founded. Within a decade Buenos Aires had more than a dozen stations, tango orchestras and radio theatre, and by 1930 Argentina counted among highest radio ownership rates outside North America. Andrea Matallana's study traces how Argentine governments regulated this new medium from 1920 to 1946.

Newspapers reported returns that came through clear and distinct, and this station, licensed as KDKA, is counted by many historians as America's first commercially licensed broadcaster.

saha-ionization-equation-1920.summary: Working at University College of Science in Calcutta, Meghnad Saha applied thermodynamics and quantum theory to gas ionisation and published in 1920 an equation relating degree of ionisation to temperature and pressure. Applied to Sun and stars, it explained why spectral lines of different elements appear at different temperatures, turning Harvard's spectral sequence into a temperature scale. Astrophysicists including Fowler, Milne and Payne built on it to measure stellar temperatures and composition. Saha later founded Institute of Nuclear Physics in Calcutta, promoted river planning and sat in parliament. His equation remains basic to plasma physics and astrophysics.

Drawn up by electrical engineers on a commission chaired by Gleb Krzhizhanovsky, championed by Lenin and approved by the Communist Party in December 1920, it aimed to restructure the Soviet economy through nationwide electrification. It called for 30 regional power plants, including ten large hydroelectric stations, to raise annual output to 8.8 billion kWh from Imperial Russia's 1.9 billion in 1913; that goal was reached in 1931, and GOELRO became Gosplan's prototype for its Five-Year Plans.

First published in English translation in New York in 1924, it did not appear in Soviet Russia until 1988; George Orwell said Brave New World must partly derive from it and acknowledged its influence on Nineteen Eighty-Four.

banting-best-insulin-1921.summary: In 1921 Banting and Best isolated insulin, and diabetes stopped being a death sentence. Eli Lilly began large-scale production that year, and Banting and Macleod shared their 1923 Nobel Prize money with Best and Collip.
